cards.explanation: The answer is the desires of the flesh, friends. Peter urges these beloved foreigners and exiles to abstain from the desires of the flesh, “…which war against your soul.” (1 Peter 2:11) Notice what's fighting here: those desires are the ones going after your soul. Warm dough has picked a few fights with me too, and I only won some of them.

The answer is False, friends. Peter says to conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God. So the answer to slander is honor and good deeds. That's a hard road, friends, and a road Peter says to walk. (1 Peter 2:12)

The answer is glorify, friends! Peter says the people slandering them may see the good deeds and glorify God “…on the day He visits us.” (1 Peter 2:12) Good deeds do the talking, and the hope is that they point people to God. Notice the word "may," because Peter leaves that part open.
The answer is the Lord, friends. Peter says to submit “…for the Lord’s sake to every human institution…” (1 Peter 2:13) The reason he gives is the Lord. That changes how a believer follows the rules.

The answer is punish wrong and praise right, friends. Peter says the governors are sent by the king “…to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.” (1 Peter 2:14) Two jobs, and they go in both directions. Praising those who do right is half of what they're sent for, and that's right there in the text.

The answer is by doing good, friends. Peter says it's God's will that “…by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men.” (1 Peter 2:15) Doing good is the way Peter names for silencing that ignorance.
The answer is True, friends! Peter says, “Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil…” (1 Peter 2:16) Freedom is a gift, and it isn't a hiding spot.

The answer is servants, friends! Peter says to live free, “live as servants of God.” (1 Peter 2:16) Free and serving go together in this verse. Freedom without a cover-up means living as God's servants.

The answer is the king, friends. Peter's short line says, “Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.” (1 Peter 2:17) Three commands, each with its own target. Honor goes to the king.

The answer is unreasonable masters, friends! Peter says to submit “…not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable.” (1 Peter 2:18) The word even is doing heavy lifting there. It isn't only the easy bosses.

The answer is True, friends. Peter says, “For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended.” (1 Peter 2:19) It's pain nobody had coming, and Peter still calls it commendable.

The answer is suffering for doing good, friends. Peter says, “But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.” (1 Peter 2:20) He sets it right beside being beaten for doing wrong. The one he calls commendable is suffering for doing good and enduring it.

The answer is an example, friends! Peter says Christ suffered for you, “…leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps…” (1 Peter 2:21) He left a trail to follow. That's what the next verses lay out.

The answer is True, friends. Peter quotes it: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” (1 Peter 2:22) No sin, and no deceit in His mouth. That's the One whose footsteps they're told to follow.

The answer is False, friends. Peter says, “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats…” (1 Peter 2:23) No retaliation and no threats. That's a lot of strength, friends, and I think it takes more than I've got.
The answer is justly, friends. Peter says Jesus “…entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.” (1 Peter 2:23) He didn't make threats. He put Himself in the hands of the One who judges justly.

The answer is die, friends. Peter says Jesus bore our sins in His body on the tree “…so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” (1 Peter 2:24) Dying to sin and living to righteousness go together in one sentence. I can't say it's easy, but I can say that's the plan in the text.

The answer is Shepherd, friends! Peter says, “you were like sheep going astray…” but now “…you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.” (1 Peter 2:25) Sheep going astray, then back to the Shepherd. That's a good place to land at the end.
